cards.front: What is exception wrapping?
cards.back: Catching a low-level exception and throwing a higher-level one that carries it as the cause
cards.extra: It preserves the stack trace while presenting an error in your abstraction's terms. Without the cause you lose the original failure.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::01 Exception Handling

cards.front: What is exception enrichment, and how does it differ from wrapping?
cards.back: Catching, adding information to the same exception, and rethrowing it — instead of creating a new one
cards.extra: Wrapping gives you a new type; enrichment keeps the original type and stack. Pick according to whether callers need the abstraction.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::01 Exception Handling

cards.front: What makes exception handling code fail-safe?
cards.back: The cleanup code itself must not throw — a failure in finally or close would mask the original exception
cards.extra: Guard cleanup with its own try/catch, and keep it minimal. This is why close() is documented as suppressing exceptions.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::01 Exception Handling

cards.front: How do you catch several exception types in one block?
cards.back: catch (IOException | SQLException e) — Java 7 multi-catch
cards.extra: The caught variable is implicitly final. Use it when the handling is identical, not as a way to avoid thinking about each case.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::01 Exception Handling

cards.front: What is the difference between a checked and an unchecked exception?
cards.back: Checked must be declared or caught (recoverable); unchecked (RuntimeException) signal programming errors
cards.extra: The compiler enforces the first. Getting the split wrong makes an API either noisy or unsafe.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::01 Exception Handling

cards.front: What is a pluggable exception handler?
cards.back: A handler object injected into a component so callers decide how its exceptions are treated
cards.extra: The component stays free of logging or UI policy; the caller supplies a strategy. Useful for libraries.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::01 Exception Handling

cards.front: Where should exceptions be logged?
cards.back: At the boundary of the application — not at every layer that catches
cards.extra: Log-and-rethrow at each level produces duplicate stack traces and hides where the failure actually originated.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::01 Exception Handling

cards.front: What is a checked exception hierarchy good for?
cards.back: Letting callers catch a family of failures with one catch, while throwing specific subtypes
cards.extra: Catch the supertype where the handling is the same; throw the subtype where the information matters.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::01 Exception Handling

cards.front: Why is naive timing of Java code misleading?
cards.back: The JIT compiles and optimises while you measure, so the first runs are slower and later ones may be eliminated
cards.extra: That is why JMH exists: it warms up, forks JVMs, and prevents dead-code elimination.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::04 Monitoring and Troubleshooting

cards.front: What is a ring buffer, and why use one?
cards.back: A preallocated circular array with read/write indices — no allocation, no GC pressure
cards.extra: Used for high-throughput queues (disruptor-style). Capacity is fixed, so writes must handle a full buffer explicitly.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::04 Monitoring and Troubleshooting

cards.front: What is micro-batching?
cards.back: Grouping many small tasks into a batch so the per-task overhead is paid once
cards.extra: It trades latency for throughput — appropriate for writes, not for interactive work.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::04 Monitoring and Troubleshooting

cards.front: Is replacing a for loop with a switch faster?
cards.back: Sometimes, but not predictably — it depends on the JIT and the data distribution
cards.extra: Modern JVMs optimise both heavily. Measure with JMH before restructuring readable code.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::04 Monitoring and Troubleshooting

cards.front: Why does memory layout matter for Java performance?
cards.back: CPU caches work in cache lines, so traversing arrays sequentially is far faster than chasing pointers
cards.extra: A plain object graph scatters across the heap. That is the reason for primitive arrays, ring buffers and struct-of-arrays designs.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::04 Monitoring and Troubleshooting

cards.front: What is a higher-order function?
cards.back: A function that takes a function as a parameter or returns one
cards.extra: In Java, that is a method taking a functional interface — Function, Predicate, Supplier.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::05 Functional Programming::04 Streams

cards.front: What is functional composition in Java?
cards.back: Combining functions into one: f.andThen(g) or f.compose(g)
cards.extra: andThen applies f first; compose applies the argument first. The order is the whole subtlety.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::05 Functional Programming::04 Streams

cards.front: What makes an interface a functional interface?
cards.back: It has exactly one abstract method — which is what allows a lambda to implement it
cards.extra: @FunctionalInterface enforces the shape. Default and static methods do not count toward the one.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::05 Functional Programming::04 Streams

cards.front: What are the two defining properties of a Java stream?
cards.back: It is lazy (nothing runs until a terminal operation) and it can be traversed only once
cards.extra: Reusing a consumed stream throws IllegalStateException. Laziness is what lets short-circuit operations skip work.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::05 Functional Programming::04 Streams

cards.front: How did Java 9 shrink String's memory footprint?
cards.back: Compact strings: a byte[] plus a coder flag, using Latin-1 when every character fits
cards.extra: An all-ASCII string halves its storage versus UTF-16 char[]. The behaviour is unchanged; only the representation is.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::09 Strings and Methods

cards.front: What is scoped access, as opposed to method chaining?
cards.back: A method returns a scope object exposing the next set of operations, rather than returning this
cards.extra: It narrows what can be called next — the builder variant that prevents invalid sequences at compile time.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::09 Strings and Methods

cards.front: When do you choose an interface over an abstract class?
cards.back: Interface for a contract many unrelated types can implement; abstract class when subclasses must share state
cards.extra: A class gets one superclass but many interfaces, so interfaces are the more flexible axis of variation.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::16 Interfaces

cards.front: What are the benefits of JPMS modules?
cards.back: Explicit dependencies, strong encapsulation (even reflection can be blocked), and a smaller runtime image
cards.extra: The module declares what it exports and what it requires; jlink then builds a runtime with only what is needed.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::04 Modules and Linking
